blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Follow the impacts of taxation through households, firms, markets and the economy as a whole, and read a worked case with figures.
blocks.repair_note: coverage gaps filled from syllabus guidance

blocks.heading: Through disposable income
blocks.text: A higher income tax takes more from each pay packet, so disposable income - what households have left to spend or save once deductions are made - falls. Because household spending tends to follow disposable income, shops and services tend to see fewer sales; where the rise is steep, some workers put in fewer hours or move income out of sight into untaxed work, weakening the very revenue the rise sought.

blocks.heading: Through prices
blocks.text: An indirect tax added at the point of sale raises the price buyers face, and the quantity demanded tends to fall. Work invented figures through: fuel duty of N$3 a litre adds N$150 to a 50-litre tank, since 3 x 50 = 150; a Swakopmund tour operator filling daily faces about N$3 300 across a 22-day month. As fares rise to cover the duty, some passengers travel less - the tax steers buying away from fuel while raising revenue for the treasury.

blocks.heading: The limits of taxation
blocks.text: Taxes change choices, and that is their limit. Set high, a duty tends to push buying into untaxed channels - cross-border trips where neighbours levy less, informal stalls, undeclared cash work - so the quantity falls by less than forecast and the revenue raised falls short of it. Drivers in Portugal near the Spanish border, for example, tend to cross to fill up where fuel duty is lower - one reason forecasts of duty revenue are written with care.

blocks.heading: Taxation and the economy as a whole
blocks.text: Beyond single households, firms and markets, taxation shapes the economy as a whole in four ways. Incentives to work and invest: where income tax rates are high, some workers may choose fewer hours or untaxed informal work, and where company tax is high compared with other countries, firms - including foreign firms deciding where to build - may invest less or invest elsewhere, which tends to slow growth. Prices: a rise in an indirect tax such as value-added tax lifts the prices of many goods at once, so it raises the general price level, while a rise in income tax that cuts household spending tends to ease the pressure on prices. The distribution of income: a progressive income tax narrows the gap between high and low incomes after tax, while a heavier reliance on value-added tax tends to widen it, because poorer households spend more of their income. Total spending, output and jobs: a general tax rise takes spending power out of the economy, so sales, output and employment tend to fall, while a tax cut tends to raise them where there is spare capacity. Which effect dominates depends on the tax chosen and the state of the economy: a value-added tax rise in a boom mainly lifts prices, while the same rise in a slump deepens the fall in sales.
